question: Which command initializes a brand-new, empty Git repository in the current directory?
explanation: git init creates a new .git directory containing all the metadata and object database needed to track the current folder as a repository.

question: What kind of version control system is Git?
explanation: Git is distributed: every clone contains the full history, so developers can commit, branch, and inspect history locally without a central server.

question: What does 'git clone <url>' primarily do?
options: Copies only the latest file versions without history
Creates an empty repo linked to the URL
Downloads a full copy of a remote repository including its history and sets up an origin remote
Pushes your local repo to the given URL
explanation: git clone downloads the entire repository (all objects and refs), checks out the default branch, and configures the source URL as the 'origin' remote.

question: Where does Git store the object database and configuration for a repository?
options: In a hidden .git directory at the repository root
explanation: All of a repo's objects, refs, and local config live in the hidden .git folder; deleting it removes Git tracking while leaving working files intact.

question: Git internally stores content as objects. Which four object types make up Git's object model?
explanation: Git's object model uses blobs (file content), trees (directory listings), commits (snapshots with metadata), and annotated tags — all addressed by SHA hashes.

question: Which command adds a file's current changes to the staging area?
explanation: git add moves changes into the staging area (index), marking exactly what will go into the next commit.

question: The staging area in Git is also commonly known as what?
explanation: The staging area is called the index; it records a snapshot of what the next commit will contain, sitting between the working tree and the repository.

question: You edit a file, run 'git add' on it, then edit it again. What happens if you commit now?
options: The commit fails with a conflict
Nothing is committed because the file changed
Only the changes that were staged (the first edit) are committed
explanation: git add snapshots the file at that moment. Later edits are unstaged, so a commit records only the staged version; the newer edit stays in the working tree.

question: Which command interactively lets you stage only selected chunks (hunks) of a modified file?
explanation: git add -p (patch mode) walks through each hunk of changes so you can stage some and leave others, enabling focused, logically-grouped commits.

question: A file is staged with 'git add'. Which command unstages it while keeping the working-tree changes intact (modern Git)?
explanation: git restore --staged removes the file from the index (unstages it) but leaves your working-tree edits untouched; the older equivalent is git reset HEAD <file>.

question: Which command records staged changes into the repository history?
explanation: git commit takes the staged snapshot and stores it permanently as a new commit object, complete with author, timestamp, and message.

question: What does the -m flag do in 'git commit -m "message"'?
options: Marks the commit as a milestone
Supplies the commit message inline without opening an editor
explanation: The -m flag lets you provide the commit message directly on the command line, skipping the default text editor.

question: What does 'git commit --amend' do?
options: Replaces the most recent commit with a new one, letting you change its message or contents
Creates a second commit on top of the last one
Merges the last two commits into main
explanation: --amend rewrites the latest commit into a brand-new commit (new SHA), useful for fixing a message or including a forgotten file — avoid it on already-pushed commits.

question: Every non-initial commit stores a reference to what, forming the history chain?
explanation: A commit points to its parent(s), so the commit graph is built by following parent links; merge commits have two or more parents.

question: Why is a Git commit SHA-1 (or SHA-256) hash considered to represent an immutable snapshot?
options: Because Git locks the file on disk
Because the hash is derived from the commit's full content including tree, parent, author, and message — any change yields a different hash
Because the server signs every commit
explanation: The commit's identity is a hash over its content and metadata. Altering anything (even the message) produces a new hash, so history can be verified but not silently edited.

question: What is a branch in Git, fundamentally?
options: A full copy of the repository
A backup of the working directory
A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit
explanation: A branch is just a movable reference (pointer) to a commit. Creating one is cheap because it only writes a small ref file, not a copy of files.

question: Which command creates a new branch and switches to it in one step (modern Git)?
explanation: git switch -c creates the branch and checks it out at once; the older equivalent is git checkout -b <name>.

question: You run 'git branch feature' but keep committing. Where do the new commits go?
options: To the branch you are currently on, not feature
explanation: git branch only creates the pointer; it does not switch to it. New commits advance whatever branch HEAD currently points to, leaving 'feature' where it was.

question: How do you safely delete a local branch that has already been merged?
explanation: git branch -d deletes a branch only if it is fully merged, guarding against losing work; -D forces deletion regardless of merge status.

question: Deleting a branch pointer that had unmerged commits seems to lose them. How can those commits usually still be recovered?
options: They cannot be recovered at all
Via the reflog and git checkout/branch on the dangling commit SHA before garbage collection removes it
explanation: The commits become unreachable but persist as dangling objects. The reflog still records the old tip SHA, so you can recreate a branch there until gc prunes them.

question: What does 'git merge' generally do?
options: Combines the histories of two branches, often creating a merge commit
Moves commits onto a new base
explanation: git merge joins two branch histories together; when they have diverged it creates a merge commit with two parents, preserving both lines of development.

question: What does 'git rebase' do to a series of commits?
options: Reapplies them on top of a different base commit, creating new commits
Merges them without any new commits
explanation: Rebase takes your commits and replays them onto a new base, producing new commits with new SHAs and yielding a linear history.

question: Which statement best contrasts merge and rebase?
options: Merge rewrites history; rebase preserves it
Merge preserves history and adds a merge commit; rebase rewrites history for a linear graph
Rebase is only for remotes; merge only for locals
explanation: Merge is non-destructive and keeps the true branching history via a merge commit; rebase moves commits to make history linear but rewrites them (new SHAs).

question: What is a 'fast-forward' merge?
options: A merge that resolves conflicts automatically by force
When the target branch has no new commits, so its pointer simply advances to the source tip without a merge commit
explanation: If the base branch hasn't diverged, Git can just move its pointer forward to the feature tip — no merge commit is needed. Use --no-ff to force one.

question: Why is rebasing commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch discouraged?
options: It rewrites commit SHAs, so collaborators' histories diverge, causing painful conflicts and duplicate commits on their next pull
explanation: Rebase replaces shared commits with new ones. Teammates still hold the originals, so their pull creates divergence and duplicates — the golden rule: don't rebase public history.

question: What is the conventional name Git gives to the default remote after cloning?
explanation: By convention the remote you cloned from is named 'origin'. It's just a short alias for the remote repository URL.

question: Which command uploads your local commits to a remote branch?
explanation: git push transfers local commits and updates the corresponding branch on the remote repository.

question: What is the key difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?
options: fetch merges automatically; pull does not
fetch downloads remote changes without merging; pull fetches and then merges (or rebases) into your branch
explanation: git fetch updates your remote-tracking refs but leaves your working branch alone. git pull is fetch followed by an automatic merge or rebase into the current branch.

question: What does a remote-tracking branch like 'origin/main' represent?
options: A local snapshot of where main was on the remote at your last fetch
A branch that lives only on the server
explanation: origin/main is a read-only pointer reflecting the remote's main as of your most recent fetch/pull; it updates only when you communicate with the remote.

question: A push is rejected as 'non-fast-forward'. What is the correct, safe response?
options: Fetch/pull to integrate the remote commits (merge or rebase), resolve conflicts, then push
Delete the remote branch and recreate it
explanation: The rejection means the remote has commits you lack. Integrate them first (pull with merge or rebase), then push. Force-push would overwrite teammates' work.

question: What does 'git revert <commit>' do?
options: Creates a new commit that undoes the changes of the target commit
explanation: git revert is a forward, non-destructive undo: it makes a new commit applying the inverse of the target commit, keeping history intact — safe on shared branches.

question: Which command moves the current branch pointer to a different commit?
explanation: git reset moves the branch (and HEAD) to a specified commit; depending on the mode it also updates the index and working tree.

question: How do 'git reset --soft', '--mixed', and '--hard' differ?
options: soft keeps index+worktree, mixed resets index but keeps worktree, hard resets index and worktree
They are aliases for the same behavior
soft deletes files, hard keeps them
Only hard moves the branch pointer
explanation: All move the branch pointer. --soft leaves staged changes and files; --mixed (default) unstages but keeps files; --hard discards both staged and working-tree changes.

question: For undoing a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch, which is preferred and why?
options: revert, because it adds an undo commit without rewriting shared history
reset --soft, because it hides the change
explanation: revert doesn't rewrite history — it appends an inverse commit — so collaborators aren't disrupted. reset rewrites history and is unsafe on shared branches.

question: You ran 'git reset --hard HEAD~3' and lost three commits of local work. What is the best recovery path?
options: Find the old HEAD SHA in the reflog and reset/checkout back to it
explanation: reset --hard discards working changes, but the previous commits remain reachable via the reflog. Locate the pre-reset SHA there and reset --hard back to it.

question: What does 'git stash' do?
options: Saves uncommitted changes aside and reverts the working directory to a clean state
explanation: git stash records your modified tracked files and staged changes onto a stack, then cleans the working directory so you can switch context.

question: Which command reapplies the most recently stashed changes and removes them from the stash stack?
explanation: git stash pop applies the top stash and then deletes it from the stack; git stash apply reapplies but keeps the entry.

question: By default, which files does 'git stash' NOT include?
explanation: Plain git stash saves tracked modifications and staged changes but leaves untracked/ignored files behind. Use -u (--include-untracked) to also stash untracked files.

question: What is the difference between 'git stash apply' and 'git stash pop'?
options: pop keeps the entry; apply removes it
apply keeps the stash entry; pop removes it after applying
apply works only on the newest stash
explanation: Both restore stashed changes, but apply leaves the stash on the stack (useful to apply to multiple branches), while pop deletes it once applied successfully.

question: You popped a stash and hit merge conflicts; the stash was NOT dropped. After resolving, how do you clean up?
options: Manually run git stash drop to remove the entry Git kept due to the conflict
explanation: When pop conflicts, Git keeps the stash entry to be safe. After you resolve and stage the changes, remove the leftover entry manually with git stash drop.

question: What does 'git cherry-pick <commit>' do?
options: Applies the changes from a specific commit onto the current branch as a new commit
explanation: cherry-pick takes one (or more) individual commits and reapplies their changes onto your current branch, creating new commits with new SHAs.

question: A cherry-picked commit gets what, compared to the original commit?
explanation: Because the commit is reapplied onto a different parent, its metadata changes and it receives a new SHA even though the code changes are the same.

question: When is cherry-pick especially useful?
options: Porting a specific bug-fix commit to a release branch without merging everything else
explanation: cherry-pick shines for selectively moving a single fix (e.g., a hotfix) to another branch such as a maintenance/release line, without bringing unrelated commits.

question: What does the -x flag add when cherry-picking?
options: It appends a line noting the original commit SHA to the message
explanation: cherry-pick -x records '(cherry picked from commit <sha>)' in the new commit message, keeping a trace back to the source commit — handy for backports.

question: Repeatedly cherry-picking commits between two long-lived branches can cause what problem later?
options: Duplicate-change conflicts when the branches are eventually merged, since the same logical change exists under two SHAs
explanation: Cherry-picking duplicates a change under a new SHA. When the branches later merge, Git may see the same content twice and produce confusing conflicts.

question: What is a Git tag most commonly used for?
options: Marking specific points in history, such as release versions like v1.0
explanation: Tags label a particular commit with a memorable name, typically to mark releases (v1.0.0) so they're easy to find and check out later.

question: Which command lists all tags in a repository?
explanation: Running git tag with no arguments prints the list of existing tags; you can filter with git tag -l '<pattern>'.

question: What is the difference between a lightweight tag and an annotated tag?
options: Lightweight tags are signed; annotated are not
Annotated tags store extra metadata (tagger, date, message) as a full object; lightweight tags are just a name pointing at a commit
explanation: An annotated tag (-a) is a full Git object with author, date, message, and optional GPG signature; a lightweight tag is merely a ref pointing to a commit.

question: By default, does 'git push' send your local tags to the remote?
options: No — tags must be pushed explicitly with git push <remote> <tag> or --tags
explanation: A normal push does not transfer tags. You push a specific tag by name, or all of them with git push --tags / git push --follow-tags.

question: You need a release tag whose authenticity can be cryptographically verified. Which tag do you create?
explanation: git tag -s creates a signed annotated tag; the GPG signature lets others verify who created the release tag with git tag -v, which lightweight tags cannot provide.

question: What does HEAD normally point to in Git?
options: The current branch (and thus the commit you have checked out)
explanation: HEAD is a symbolic reference to your current branch, which in turn points to a commit; it tells Git what you have checked out.

question: What does 'HEAD~1' refer to?
options: The first parent of HEAD (one commit back)
explanation: HEAD~1 (or HEAD~) means the commit one step back along the first-parent line — the parent of the currently checked-out commit.

question: What is a 'detached HEAD' state?
options: HEAD points directly at a specific commit instead of a branch
explanation: When you check out a commit (or tag) directly, HEAD references that commit rather than a branch. New commits made here aren't on any branch.

question: Why can commits made in a detached HEAD state be lost?
options: They belong to no branch, so switching away leaves them unreferenced and eligible for garbage collection
They are pushed to origin automatically
explanation: Without a branch pointing to them, detached-HEAD commits are only reachable via the reflog. Once you switch branches they can be pruned by gc if not saved.

question: You made several valuable commits in a detached HEAD, then ran 'git switch main'. How do you preserve that work?
options: Create a branch at the detached commit — e.g. git branch <name> <sha> using the SHA from reflog or the switch warning
explanation: Git warns and prints the detached commit SHA when you leave. Create a branch there (git branch/switch -c <name> <sha>), or recover the SHA from the reflog.

question: When does a merge conflict occur?
options: When you push to a remote
When the same lines of a file were changed differently in the two branches being combined
explanation: Git auto-merges non-overlapping changes. A conflict arises when both branches modified the same region of a file and Git can't decide which to keep.

question: In a conflicted file, what do the '<<<<<<<', '=======', and '>>>>>>>' markers separate?
options: Your current-branch changes from the incoming-branch changes
explanation: The markers delimit conflict hunks: content between <<<<<<< and ======= is HEAD/current, and between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming branch.

question: After manually editing conflicted files to resolve them, what must you do to complete the merge?
options: Stage the resolved files (git add) and then commit (or git merge --continue)
explanation: Removing markers isn't enough — you must git add the resolved files to tell Git the conflict is settled, then commit to finalize the merge.

question: Which command aborts an in-progress merge and returns to the pre-merge state?
explanation: git merge --abort cancels a conflicted merge and restores the working tree and index to how they were before the merge began.

question: What does enabling 'git rerere' provide during repeated conflict resolution?
options: It forces one side to win
It records how you resolved a conflict and auto-reapplies the same resolution when the identical conflict recurs
explanation: rerere (reuse recorded resolution) remembers your manual conflict resolutions and replays them for identical conflicts later — very handy during long-lived rebases.

question: What does 'git log' display?
options: The commit history of the current branch
explanation: git log shows the sequence of commits reachable from HEAD, newest first, with author, date, and message for each.

question: Which option condenses each commit in the log to a single line?
explanation: git log --oneline prints an abbreviated SHA and the first line of each commit message, giving a compact overview of history.

question: Which command visualizes branch and merge structure as an ASCII graph?
explanation: git log --graph draws lines connecting commits to show branching and merging; it's often combined with --oneline --all for a full picture.

question: How can you see the actual code changes (diffs) introduced by each commit in the log?
explanation: git log -p (or --patch) shows the patch/diff for each commit, letting you review exactly what changed line by line through history.

question: Which git log invocation finds commits whose diff added or removed a specific string, useful for tracking when code was introduced?
explanation: The pickaxe git log -S searches the content of changes, listing commits where the count of the given string changed — ideal for locating when a line appeared or vanished.

question: With no arguments, what does 'git diff' show?
options: Differences between the working tree and the staging area (unstaged changes)
explanation: Plain git diff compares your working-directory files against the index, revealing changes you have made but not yet staged.

question: Which command shows the changes that are staged and ready to be committed?
explanation: git diff --staged (alias --cached) compares the index against the last commit (HEAD), showing exactly what your next commit will record.

question: What does 'git diff branchA..branchB' show?
options: Changes that turn branchA's tip into branchB's tip
explanation: The two-dot form compares the two endpoint snapshots, showing the net difference from branchA's tip to branchB's tip.

question: How do you view the diff of what a specific commit changed relative to its parent?
explanation: git diff <commit>^ <commit> compares a commit to its parent; git show <commit> is a convenient shortcut that displays the same patch plus metadata.

question: What is the difference between 'git diff A..B' and 'git diff A...B'?
options: Two dots compares the two tips directly; three dots compares B against the merge-base (common ancestor) of A and B
Two dots only works on merges
explanation: A..B diffs the endpoints. A...B diffs from the common ancestor (merge-base) to B, i.e., what B changed since the branches diverged — matching how PRs are shown.

question: What is the purpose of a .gitignore file?
options: To specify intentionally untracked files that Git should ignore
explanation: .gitignore lists patterns for files/directories Git should not track, such as build artifacts, dependencies, and secrets, keeping them out of the repository.

question: Which pattern in .gitignore ignores all files ending in .log?
explanation: The glob *.log matches any file with the .log extension in the directories where the rule applies.

question: A file is already tracked by Git. You add it to .gitignore. What happens?
options: It stays tracked; .gitignore only affects untracked files, so you must git rm --cached it to stop tracking
explanation: .gitignore is only consulted for untracked files. To stop tracking an already-committed file you must remove it from the index with git rm --cached and commit.

question: What does a leading '!' do in a .gitignore pattern, e.g. '!important.log'?
options: Negates a previous ignore rule, re-including the matched file
explanation: A '!' prefix negates an earlier pattern, un-ignoring the file — though it cannot re-include a file if its parent directory is entirely ignored.

question: A pattern with a trailing slash and a leading slash, like '/build/', means what?
options: Ignore build anywhere in the tree
Ignore only the 'build' directory located at the repository root, not nested build folders
explanation: A leading slash anchors the pattern to the .gitignore's location (repo root here), and the trailing slash restricts the match to directories — so only the root-level build/ is ignored.

question: What are Git hooks in a repository?
options: Scripts that Git runs automatically at certain points in the Git lifecycle
explanation: Hooks are executable scripts triggered by Git events (e.g., before a commit or push), letting you automate checks or actions in the workflow.

question: In which directory do a repository's hook scripts live by default?
explanation: Sample and active hook scripts reside in .git/hooks. Git runs the appropriately named executable there when the corresponding event fires.

question: Which hook runs before a commit is created and can block it by exiting non-zero?
explanation: The pre-commit hook fires before the commit is recorded; a non-zero exit aborts the commit, making it ideal for linting or running quick tests.

question: Why are hooks in .git/hooks not shared automatically when someone clones the repo?
options: The .git directory (including hooks) is local and not part of the tracked, cloned content
explanation: Hooks live inside the local .git folder, which isn't versioned or transferred on clone. Teams share hooks via a tracked directory plus core.hooksPath or a tool like Husky.

question: What distinguishes client-side hooks from server-side hooks like pre-receive?
options: Client-side hooks run on the developer's machine (commit, push events); server-side hooks like pre-receive run on the remote to accept or reject pushed updates
explanation: Client-side hooks (pre-commit, pre-push) run locally and are easily bypassed. Server-side hooks (pre-receive, update, post-receive) run on the server and can enforce policy that clients cannot skip.

question: What is a Git submodule in a project?
options: A repository embedded inside another repository at a specific commit
explanation: A submodule lets you include another Git repository within your project, pinned to a specific commit, while keeping the two histories separate.

question: Which command adds a submodule to a repository?
explanation: git submodule add <url> [path] registers the external repo as a submodule and records it in the .gitmodules file.

question: After cloning a repo that contains submodules, why might the submodule directories be empty?
options: Submodule contents aren't fetched by default; you must run git submodule update --init --recursive (or clone with --recurse-submodules)
explanation: A normal clone records submodule references but leaves their folders empty. Initialize and fetch them with git submodule update --init --recursive.

question: What does the parent repository actually store for each submodule?
options: A full copy of the submodule's files
A pointer to a specific commit SHA in the submodule's repository
explanation: The superproject records the exact commit (gitlink) each submodule should be checked out to, so everyone gets a consistent, pinned version.

question: You updated code inside a submodule and committed there. Why does the parent repo still show changes?
options: The parent tracks the submodule's commit SHA, so you must commit the updated pointer in the parent repo too
explanation: Committing in the submodule advances its HEAD; the parent still points at the old SHA. You must stage and commit the new submodule commit reference in the superproject.

question: What is 'git bisect' used for?
options: Finding the commit that introduced a bug via binary search through history
explanation: git bisect performs a binary search across the commit range, quickly narrowing down which commit first introduced a regression.

question: Which two states do you mark to begin a bisect session?
options: one good commit and one bad commit
explanation: You tell Git a known-good commit and a known-bad commit; it then checks out midpoints for you to test until the first bad commit is isolated.

question: During a manual bisect, after testing each checked-out commit, what do you tell Git?
options: git bisect good or git bisect bad, based on whether the bug is present
explanation: You label each midpoint commit good or bad; Git uses your answers to halve the remaining range until it reports the first bad commit.

question: How can bisect be fully automated?
options: With git bisect run <script>, where the script's exit code signals good (0) or bad (non-zero)
explanation: git bisect run executes your test script at each step; exit code 0 marks the commit good and non-zero marks it bad, letting Git find the culprit hands-free.

question: After a bisect session identifies the bad commit, what should you run to return HEAD to its original position?
explanation: git bisect reset ends the session and restores HEAD (and the working tree) to where you were before bisecting began; forgetting it leaves you on a bisect checkout.

question: What does 'git reflog' record?
options: A local history of where HEAD and branch references have pointed over time
explanation: The reflog tracks updates to HEAD and branch tips locally, so you can see and return to previous states even after resets or rebases.

question: Is the reflog stored locally or shared with remotes?
options: Stored locally only, not pushed or cloned
explanation: The reflog is a per-repository local record; it isn't transferred by push, fetch, or clone, so it reflects only your own actions.

question: How does the reflog help recover from a bad 'git reset --hard'?
options: It shows the SHA of the commit HEAD pointed to before the reset, which you can reset/checkout back to
explanation: Every HEAD move is logged, so git reflog reveals the pre-reset commit SHA. You can then git reset --hard <sha> to restore the lost state.

question: What does the reference 'HEAD@{2}' mean in reflog syntax?
options: Where HEAD pointed two moves ago in the reflog
explanation: HEAD@{n} addresses a prior position of HEAD by reflog index; HEAD@{2} is where HEAD was two recorded moves ago, distinct from HEAD~2 (two parents back).

question: Why might a 'lost' commit eventually become truly unrecoverable even though it once appeared in the reflog?
options: Reflog entries expire (default ~90 days for reachable, 30 for unreachable) and git gc then prunes the now-unreferenced objects
explanation: Reflog entries expire after a configurable time (gc.reflogExpire). Once expired, the commit is unreferenced, and a garbage-collection run can permanently prune it.

question: In a feature-branch workflow, where is new feature work typically done?
options: On a dedicated branch created off main, then merged back via a pull request
explanation: Feature-branch workflow isolates each change on its own branch off main; the branch is reviewed and merged (often through a pull/merge request) when ready.

question: What is the main idea of trunk-based development?
options: Developers integrate small changes into a single main branch (trunk) frequently, avoiding long-lived branches
Every feature has a permanent branch
explanation: Trunk-based development favors short-lived branches and frequent merges to a shared trunk, reducing merge pain and supporting continuous integration.

question: In the classic Git Flow model, what is the 'develop' branch used for?
options: Integrating completed features as the ongoing next-release line, separate from the stable main/master
explanation: Git Flow uses develop as the integration branch for features heading to the next release, while main/master holds production-ready, released code.

question: What is the purpose of a 'hotfix' branch in Git Flow?
options: Quickly patching a production issue by branching from main, then merging back to both main and develop
explanation: A hotfix branch is cut from main to fix an urgent production bug; the fix is merged back into main (and tagged) and also into develop to keep lines in sync.

question: Why do many teams prefer trunk-based development with feature flags over long-lived feature branches?
options: It removes the need for code review
Short-lived integration reduces large, painful merges and merge-conflict drift, while feature flags let unfinished code ship dark and be toggled on later
explanation: Long-lived branches drift far from main and cause huge, risky merges. Trunk-based work integrates frequently; feature flags keep incomplete features hidden until enabled, decoupling deploy from release.
